summary.text: A trajectory describes the physical path a moving object follows across space over a period of time.
While simple paths in a vacuum form parabolas or ellipses, motion in nature often involves extra forces like air drag or radiation pressure.
Newton's theory of motion grew into classical mechanics, which helps explain and predict an enormous range of phenomena, including the orbits of planets.

facts.label: Parabolic Path
facts.value: Shape of short throws under uniform gravity in a vacuum

facts.label: Orbital Shapes
facts.value: Ellipses or hyperbolas created by spherical gravitational fields

facts.label: Ballistics Focus
facts.value: Calculates motion while accounting for air drag and gravity variations

facts.label: Launch Speed
facts.value: Initial velocity at which an object leaves its origin

items.prompt: An astronaut on the Moon throws a small rock a short distance across the airless surface. What geometric shape best describes the path the rock takes?

options.label: A straight vertical line rising and falling
A perfect, endless circle
A parabola
A hyperbola

items.explain: In a simplified model with a uniform gravitational field and no air drag, such as throwing a rock short distances on the Moon, the trajectory is a parabola.

items.prompt: A space probe travels near a large, perfectly spherical planet with no atmosphere. If gravity is the only force acting on the probe, what shape will its path take?

options.label: A conic section, such as an ellipse or hyperbola
A uniform parabola curved toward the horizon
A spiraling circle that steadily shrinks
A straight line that bends into a right angle

items.explain: In the gravitational field of a spherically symmetrical mass, the moving object's trajectory is a conic section, typically an ellipse or hyperbola.

items.prompt: A comet passes very close to the Sun. Why might its real path differ from a pure gravitational orbit?

options.label: Air resistance in deep space slows the comet down significantly.
Solar wind and radiation pressure exert additional forces on it.
The comet loses its mass, causing gravity to stop acting on it.
Classical mechanics does not apply to objects larger than rocks.

items.explain: When a comet passes close to the Sun, non-gravitational influences like solar wind and radiation pressure modify its orbit.

items.prompt: Why does a rock thrown on the Moon follow a simple parabola more closely than one thrown on Earth?

options.label: Its lighter gravity makes rocks lose weight in flight
Rocks keep more of their speed when launched there
Its surface is flatter than any terrain on Earth
It has almost no atmosphere to add air drag

items.explain: Air drag and other effects can change a trajectory, but in a near vacuum such as on the Moon the simple parabolic path is essentially correct.

items.prompt: A kicker wants to send a ball as far as possible at a fixed launch speed on the airless Moon. Which launch angle does that?

options.label: Halfway between flat and straight up, at 45°
As steep as possible, nearly straight up
Nearly flat, close to the ground
About 60 degrees, steeper than halfway

items.explain: For a given launch speed in a uniform field without drag, the maximum range comes when the initial angle is 45°.

items.prompt: According to Hamiltonian mechanics, what two quantities must be known at the same time to fully define an object's trajectory?

options.label: Its launch angle and drag coefficient
Its mass and acceleration
Its position and momentum
Its elevation angle and time in flight

items.explain: In Hamiltonian mechanics within classical physics, a complete trajectory is defined simultaneously by position and momentum.
